title: Awesome
text:
In Jules Verne’s wildest imagination, the technology that would send humanity starward was already familiar on Earth. The launching mechanism for the American rocket, in Verne’s 1865 novel From the Earth to the Moon , is—of all things—a colossal cannon. The speed required to reach the lunar surface, he reasoned, would require a gunshot of a launch. So in Vernian terms, a starship was not merely launched but “fired” into space.

 I’ve been thinking of Verne today as I watched the video (then watched it again, and again) of SpaceX’s latest history-making maneuver. Yesterday, for the first time ever, engineers successfully pulled off a midair landing —using the company’s Mechazilla tower’s “chopstick” arms to snatch a starship the size of a skyscraper out of the sky after it had spent the past 22 hours in Earth’s orbit. Up until this point, Mechazilla’s chopsticks had caught boosters after launch—that is, the part of the rocket that detaches—but never ships themselves.

 You really do have to watch the video for yourself, and when you do, try to remember this: Starship 42—the largest and most powerful rocket in the world—just successfully launched, went into orbit, took 14 victory laps around the Earth at some 17,000 miles per hour, deploying more than two dozen Starlink satellites as it went, before careening into our atmosphere then swiveling upright so it could glide gently into a pair of robot arms waiting below.

 Every aspect of what took place is unbelievably hard to achieve, but let’s begin with the absolute violence of reentry. A rocket in orbit goes fast, so fast it is difficult to visualize, something like 20 times faster than the speed of sound, and certainly faster than a bullet (or, for that matter, a cannonball). When the starship approaches the Earth’s atmosphere, traveling five miles a second, several things happen in quick succession: Engineers fire a single engine against the direction of travel, in order to steer it back toward Earth belly-first. This move is less about slowing the ship down—it barely does—and more about achieving the right orientation so that the heat shield coating the belly of the starship can double as, essentially, a giant brake against the air of the atmosphere.

 Only the thinnest traces of air wisp through space, and therefore a rocket in orbit encounters no heat-producing friction. But as the ship suddenly collides with the air of the atmosphere, an enormous shock wave forms. Friction with the atmosphere heats up the air around the ship until it turns into superhot plasma, which envelopes the starship in a terrifying-gorgeous orange glow. (The glow makes a bit more sense when you realize that the plasma approaches 13,000 degrees Fahrenheit, hotter than the surface of the sun.) From there, the ship is still falling Earthward horizontally, and slowing down as it does so.

 Yesterday, a crowd assembled in Texas to see if SpaceX could actually land it. They first heard a sonic boom—people cheered at the sound—shortly before Starship 42 appeared, a black obelisk belly-flopping its way through the clouds. What happened next was the flip maneuver that resembled, as SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell put it , “alien-level technology.” When the ship was less than one mile from the ground, it had to go from falling flat to falling in an upright position, so that the chopstick arms of the tower below could catch it. To do this, engineers re-lit the ship’s engines and used sophisticated steering mechanisms to swing the ship vertical. Seconds later—roughly 21 seconds by my count—the rocket floated down to the two long arms of the tower with improbable elegance. “It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman posted on X after the successful landing. And it really was.

 It is not an exaggeration to say that almost no one believed this was possible. Even SpaceX’s most devoted engineers had their doubts. The aerospace engineer Tom Mueller, whom Musk hired as SpaceX’s first employee in 2002, recently appeared on a podcast where he described the meeting, several years ago, where Musk first presented the idea of plucking a rocket out of midair as it landed. The idea was, “ We’re going to catch it in the air on chopsticks, like catching a fly with chopsticks ,” Mueller recalled, “and we all just rolled our eyes like This is crazy. There’s just no way. ” He went on: “Some of us did not believe it could be done.”

 They were wrong, and beautifully so. (Musk, who five years ago teased the idea of the chopstick landing by tweeting a GIF of Mr. Miyagi, reported yesterday that he hugged Starship 42 upon its return.) The lesson for Mueller—and this was something he said even before yesterday’s triumph—was this: “It’s not hype. He’s going to build it. I believe if it’s possible, it will be solved. And it might take longer than Elon thinks, but he will solve it.” (I should note here that it is possible to acknowledge two things at once: that Musk is an omnidirectional boor, and also that he builds awesome rockets.)

 Our species has never struggled to dream up the impossible. But humans are often ambivalent, and cynical, when technological change inevitably arrives. This is understandable. Life is so short, and most tech revolutions and their consequences span generations. Even the most dedicated historians simply don’t have the time or perspective to see clearly and completely what it means for humanity when our most daring technological ideas are realized.

 Long before Verne, Cyrano de Bergerac invented his own fictional rocket—also powered by gunpowder—in his posthumously published 1657 novel, The Other World . But it is Americans who tend to see the impossible as a kind of dare. Uncommon audacity is, to paraphrase Verne, an American birthright. (Although Musk is South African by birth, he is American by choice.) Verne’s writing was laced with satire about the national character, a fact that is sometimes ignored today. More recently Verne is remembered mostly for his prescience—Neil Armstrong always delighted in the fact that Verne’s space voyagers eventually splashed down in the Pacific Ocean, just as he did when he returned from the moon.

 But it’s worth lingering on the cynicism underlying Verne’s satirical views today. Where Italians had their music and Germans had their philosophy, Verne wrote in From the Earth to the Moon , Americans had their guns. The novel was premised on the idea that, when the Civil War ended, Americans would mourn the end of fighting because they didn’t have a reason to focus their ingenuity on the making of ever-more-powerful weaponry. And so, on that “sad and melancholy” day that peace arrived following a war that killed hundreds of thousands of Americans, a small group of them decided to pivot from guns to the moon—a dream that would enable them to engineer the impossible with a “Platonic kind of artillery.” (Verne’s work was prescient not just on a technical level, it turned out: He also anticipated the commercialization of science.)

 In Verne’s imagination, Americans went to the moon not because they dared to do the impossible, but because they wanted to fire a cosmically powerful weapon. In reality, when Americans reached the moon, they left behind a stainless-steel plaque bearing the following inscription: Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969 A.D. We came in peace for all mankind. 

 Back home on Earth, people sometimes lament those among us who can’t help but gaze skyward. Why go to space , they ask, when there is so much work to be done here on this planet? I’d like to say this attitude is understandable, but the truth is that I’ve always seen it as reflecting a false binary, one that imposes limits on what we can achieve and one that assumes there is nothing more to be gained from a tremendous technological achievement than the achievement itself.

 One of the tricks that technology plays on us is that it sometimes leaves the impression of permanence—that a machine or system that works fairly well, or even extraordinarily well, in a certain way, is proof of an end state. But every technological system that becomes obsolete does so because it is replaced with a wholly new way of understanding the world and humanity’s place in it. We learned that sound waves can be recorded and played back, that electricity can be harnessed, that cathode rays allow us see through solid matter, that chemists can cure epidemics of childhood death, that the telephone is portable, that the telephone is in fact a computer , that you can lift up a glass rectangle and use it to see someone—and talk to them in real time!—through the glowing portal of its screen, and that the machines themselves can talk. This is not to say that every technological change is inherently good for humanity, because of course it is not. The resilience of our species, our impressive adaptability in the face of constant change, is one of our superpowers. It is also the quality that numbs us to the impositions of new technology that we ought to reject. However, human resilience cuts the other way, too. It can dull our sense of wonder about what is possible when humanity attempts to do something that almost no one believes can be done. This weekend, SpaceX achieved the impossible. Tomorrow, someone else will, too.
